title: Become a Young European Ambassador: Join the YEA Network and Connect Youth Across Europe and the Eastern Neighbourhood
summary: The Young European Ambassadors (YEA) initiative is a youth network that brings together young people from the European Union and the Eastern Partnership countries to promote youth participation, awareness, dialogue, solidarity, and connections across borders. The initiative is part of the work of EU NEIGHBOURS east , which provides news, information and opportunities relating to the European Union s cooperation with its Eastern partners: Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Georgia, the Republic of Moldova and Ukraine . For young people interested in European affairs, youth engagement, community initiatives, democracy, human rights, environmental issues, gender equality, international cooperation and cross-border networking, the Young European Ambassadors initiative provides an opportunity to become part of a growing regional community. The network is celebrating its 10th anniversary in 2026 , marking a decade of youth-led activities, connections, campaigns, community initiatives and cooperation. What Is the Young European Ambassadors Initiative? The Young European Ambassadors initiative is a network that gives young people a platform to become active in their communities while connecting with peers across the Eastern Neighbourhood and the European Union. Since its launch, YEAs have worked to raise awareness about the EU s partnership with its Eastern neighbours, promote shared values and communicate opportunities available to young people. The initiative has also supported youth-led activities addressing issues such as: Democracy and civic participation Human rights Environmental protection Gender equality Youth empowerment European integration and cooperation Community development Solidarity and social engagement Awareness of educational and professional opportunities Cross-border youth networking Rather than being limited to one particular type of activity, the YEA network provides a space where young people can develop connections and participate in initiatives that respond to issues affecting their communities and the wider region. A Decade of Young European Ambassadors The YEA network was officially launched on 16 June 2016 , when the first 100 Young European Ambassadors were selected from the six Eastern partner countries and the European Union. The six Eastern partner countries represented in the initiative are: Armenia Azerbaijan Belarus Georgia Republic of Moldova Ukraine The initiative began with activities designed to connect young people with their communities and increase awareness of EU values, cooperation and opportunities. One of the early activities involved visits to schools across the Republic of Moldova, where Young European Ambassadors engaged with students and raised awareness about European Union values and opportunities. Over the following decade, the network expanded substantially, developing a broader regional and international community. Young European Ambassadors and Regional Cooperation An important part of the YEA initiative has been creating connections among young people from different countries. For example, in 2019, activities marking the 10th anniversary of the Eastern Partnership brought 100 Young European Ambassadors to Brussels for the Eastern Partnership 10th Anniversary Launch Event. The YEAs organised a flashmob in front of the European Commission, featuring national costumes and the flags of the six Eastern partner countries and the European Union. Similar activities were also organised by Young European Ambassadors across the six partner countries. These activities demonstrate the network s emphasis on youth-to-youth connections, cultural exchange, public engagement and regional cooperation. Community Engagement and Grassroots Impact The Young European Ambassadors network has a strong grassroots dimension. YEAs have participated in activities intended to bring information, opportunities and discussions closer to young people in local communities. Through school visits, campaigns, public activities, community initiatives and youth engagement, members have helped create opportunities for young people to discuss issues affecting their societies. This grassroots approach allows Young European Ambassadors to connect broader European and regional discussions with local communities. The initiative s activities have included work around: Youth participation Education and learning opportunities Community engagement Awareness campaigns Human rights Democracy Environmental issues Gender equality European cooperation Social solidarity Supporting Solidarity and Youth Action The network has also responded to major developments affecting communities across the region. Following Russia s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Young European Ambassadors across the partner countries and the European Union mobilised solidarity activities. These included awareness-raising events, solidarity actions and volunteer initiatives supporting Ukraine. The YEA network has subsequently continued to provide a platform for youth engagement around issues affecting the region. The initiative also highlights the importance of youth voices in conversations surrounding European enlargement, particularly following applications for EU membership by Ukraine, Moldova and Georgia in 2022. A Growing International Youth Network The scale of the YEA network has grown considerably since its establishment. According to EU NEIGHBOURS east, as the network reaches its tenth anniversary in 2026, it has almost 1,000 active members , while more than 3,000 people have served as Young European Ambassadors since the initiative began in 2016 . This provides current and former members with an extensive network of people who have participated in youth initiatives across the Eastern Neighbourhood and Europe. The network therefore extends beyond individual activities. Members can develop relationships with peers, alumni and other participants whose experiences can continue to be valuable after particular YEA activities have ended. What Do Young European Ambassadors Do? Young European Ambassadors have participated in a wide range of activities depending on their communities, interests and the issues being addressed. Examples of YEA engagement include: 1. Raising Awareness YEAs communicate information about the European Union, its partnership with Eastern neighbours and opportunities available to young people. This can involve conversations, campaigns, public activities, educational engagement and digital communication. 2. Supporting Community Initiatives Young European Ambassadors can participate in activities that address issues within their communities. This grassroots dimension enables members to translate broader ideas into practical local engagement. 3. Promoting Democracy and Human Rights The YEA network has supported awareness around democracy and human rights, including efforts to keep these issues visible within youth and community discussions. 4. Environmental Engagement Young European Ambassadors have also participated in activities connected to environmental awareness and the importance of protecting the environment. 5. Promoting Gender Equality Gender equality has been among the issues addressed through YEA campaigns and activities. 6. Building Youth Connections A central part of the initiative is connecting young people from different countries and communities. These relationships can create opportunities for collaboration, knowledge exchange and continued engagement. 7. Supporting Solidarity The network has demonstrated its capacity to organise solidarity activities and volunteer initiatives in response to regional developments. Examples of YEA Experiences The 10th-anniversary campaign highlights experiences from current and former Young European Ambassadors, illustrating the different ways participants have engaged with the initiative. One example comes from Dmytro , whose highlighted experience involved bringing opportunities closer to young people in Poltava and engaging youth councils and student self-governments. His experience demonstrates how YEA participation can involve direct work with youth organisations and local institutions. Another example comes from Tatevik , who highlighted a 2019 Human Rights Day campaign involving free morning coffee for passers-by as a way of creating everyday conversations around human rights. Her experience also reflects the network s broader emphasis on creating meaningful conversations through accessible community activities. The initiative also features the experience of Ambroise , who described gaining a strong network of people, support and experiences that continued to remain valuable after his participation. His experience illustrates how relationships developed through the network can extend beyond individual activities and locations. The Importance of the YEA Network in 2026 The tenth anniversary provides an opportunity to reflect on the development of the initiative while looking toward its future. Over ten years, the YEA network has moved from its initial group of 100 ambassadors to a community involving thousands of current and former members. Today, YEAs remain active across the region and within the European Union. Their activities include: Promoting awareness of EU opportunities Supporting solidarity with Ukraine Discussing European enlargement Raising awareness of democracy Highlighting human rights issues Connecting young people across countries Supporting youth-led activities Strengthening community networks The anniversary campaign is built around the theme of connections that last , highlighting friendships, networks, experiences and community relationships developed through the initiative. Why Join the Young European Ambassadors Network? Becoming part of a youth network such as the YEA initiative can provide opportunities to participate in activities beyond one s immediate community. Participants can potentially benefit from exposure to: Regional and International Networking The network connects young people from the Eastern partner countries and the European Union, creating opportunities to meet peers with different backgrounds and experiences. title: Impact100 DC Fellowship 2026: Fully Funded Philanthropy Fellowship for Women Ages 21–39 in the Washington, DC Region
summary: The Impact100 DC Fellowship 2026 offers an opportunity for women between the ages of 21 and 39 who are interested in philanthropy and community impact but may not have the financial resources to become full members of Impact100 DC. The fellowship allows participants to experience collective giving firsthand , take part in the organization s grant review process, contribute to community activities, and develop their leadership and philanthropic skills. Fellows become full members from the beginning of the fellowship at no cost , allowing them to participate alongside other Impact100 DC members without having to pay the standard membership contribution. Applications for the fellowship are currently open, with applications due October 15, 2026 . What Is the Impact100 DC Fellowship? The Impact100 DC Fellowship is designed for women who want to learn about philanthropy through direct participation rather than simply observing from the sidelines. The program gives Fellows the opportunity to become actively involved in how philanthropic resources are distributed and how grants can contribute to positive change in the community. Through the fellowship, participants experience the process of collective giving and help shape how Impact100 DC grants affect the community. Rather than requiring Fellows to make the standard financial contribution associated with membership, the fellowship provides qualifying participants with full membership at no cost. This creates an opportunity for women who are interested in philanthropy but may not have the financial resources to join Impact100 DC through the regular membership route. Experience Collective Giving Firsthand One of the central features of the Impact100 DC Fellowship is the opportunity to experience collective giving directly. Collective giving involves people coming together to pool resources and participate collectively in decisions about how those resources are distributed through grants. For Fellows, this means gaining practical exposure to the grantmaking process and understanding how philanthropic decisions can influence organizations and communities. Fellows are not passive participants. They are expected to become involved in the organization s activities and contribute to the grant review process. Full Membership From Day One at No Cost A major feature of the fellowship is that Fellows become full members from the beginning of the fellowship at no cost . The program emphasizes that Fellows do not simply observe Impact100 DC s activities. Instead, they participate as members and contribute to the organization s work. Fellows are expected to: Serve on at least one grant review committee. Contribute their skills to outreach, events, or communications. Connect with Impact100 DC members. Attend events and member activities. Participate actively in the community. Develop their leadership experience through involvement in the organization. This structure allows Fellows to gain practical experience while also contributing their own skills and perspectives. Grant Review Committee Participation Participation in the grant review process is a required component of the fellowship. Each Fellow must serve on at least one grant review committee . This gives Fellows direct experience with an important aspect of philanthropy: reviewing grant opportunities and participating in the process through which philanthropic resources can support community organizations. For women interested in nonprofit organizations, social impact, community development, charitable giving, or philanthropy, this experience can provide an opportunity to better understand how grantmaking works in practice. Opportunities to Contribute Skills Fellows can also contribute their individual skills to areas such as: Outreach Events Communications This means the fellowship is not limited to grant review. Participants can use their existing professional, academic, creative, organizational, communication, or community-building skills while gaining new experience through their involvement. This support allows Fellows to participate as full members without paying the standard membership cost. Leadership Development By participating in committees, events, outreach, communications, and member activities, Fellows can develop leadership and organizational experience. Understanding Grantmaking Serving on a grant review committee can help Fellows understand how grantmaking processes operate and how philanthropic resources can be directed toward community needs. title: TradeRoots Africa 2026–2027: ICC Programme Helping African SMEs Become Export-Ready and Access Regional and Global Markets
summary: African small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) seeking to expand beyond their domestic markets can now apply for TradeRoots Africa , an initiative of the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) Centre of Entrepreneurship designed to help businesses become export-ready and compete more effectively across African and international markets. The programme is particularly focused on helping African SMEs navigate the practical challenges associated with regional and international trade, including export compliance, trade documentation, market access, digital trade, logistics, customs, trade finance, mentorship and business development. Applications for TradeRoots Africa are currently open, with the application deadline set for 15 October 2026 . The programme is scheduled to officially launch in November 2026 and continue through August 2027 . What Is TradeRoots Africa? TradeRoots Africa is an SME-focused trade development programme established by the ICC Centre of Entrepreneurship to help African businesses translate regional and continental trade opportunities into practical business growth. The initiative was launched at the 2025 B20 Summit in South Africa and is designed around the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) and the Regional Economic Communities (RECs) . Rather than focusing only on theoretical knowledge about international trade, TradeRoots Africa takes a practical approach. The programme aims to help participating businesses develop the knowledge, capabilities, connections and resources needed to move towards actual export activity. According to the ICC, African SMEs represent approximately 90% of businesses on the continent and employ around 70% of the workforce , yet fewer than 20% formally export. The programme therefore seeks to address some of the barriers preventing otherwise viable African businesses from accessing regional and international markets. Why TradeRoots Africa Was Created Expanding a business into another country can involve considerably more than simply finding international customers. African SMEs can face multiple interconnected barriers when attempting to enter regional and global markets. These include: High costs associated with international trade. Complex regulatory and customs requirements. Limited access to digital trade tools. Infrastructure constraints. Difficulty accessing appropriate financing. Limited knowledge of export procedures. Challenges understanding regional and international markets. Limited access to potential buyers and business networks. The ICC notes that these challenges are interconnected, meaning that addressing one obstacle in isolation may not be sufficient to turn an SME into a successful exporter. TradeRoots Africa therefore brings several forms of support together in a structured programme intended to take participating businesses from foundational trade knowledge towards export acceleration. The Six Key Pillars of TradeRoots Africa TradeRoots Africa is structured around six major areas of support. Together, these pillars are intended to provide participating SMEs with practical capabilities for regional and international trade. 1. Trade Knowledge and Market Access Businesses will receive support in understanding trade requirements and identifying opportunities to access markets beyond their domestic market. This pillar is particularly important for SMEs that may have a product or service with growth potential but lack sufficient knowledge of export procedures, market requirements and regional trade opportunities. 2. Trade Finance Access to finance can be an important factor in a company s ability to enter new markets. TradeRoots Africa incorporates trade finance into its support framework, helping businesses develop greater readiness around financing requirements associated with international trade. 3. Logistics, Customs and Air Transport Cross-border trade requires businesses to understand how goods move between markets and how customs and logistical processes affect exports. The programme therefore includes logistics, customs and air transport as one of its six central pillars. 4. Digital Trade Tools Digital technologies are increasingly important for businesses seeking customers and opportunities beyond their domestic markets. TradeRoots Africa includes digital trade tools among its core areas of support, with later programme activities also focusing on e-commerce and related digital capabilities. 5. Mentorship Participating SMEs will have access to mentorship as part of the programme s broader support ecosystem. Mentorship can provide businesses with practical guidance as they work through trade-related challenges and develop their internationalisation strategies. 6. Business Development The programme also focuses on business development, helping participating SMEs strengthen their commercial readiness and move towards concrete market opportunities. These six pillars collectively form the foundation of the TradeRoots Africa SME support system. How the TradeRoots Africa Programme Works TradeRoots Africa is organised into three progressive tiers . The structure means that participation can develop from foundational trade education to more specialised support and ultimately to export acceleration. Tier 1: Trade Foundations Period: November 2026 – March 2027 The first tier is designed to establish the fundamental knowledge SMEs need before entering regional and international markets. The ICC states that 1,000 SMEs will participate in this stage. Participants will learn about areas including: Export compliance. Trade documentation. AfCFTA. Regional trade fundamentals. Other foundational aspects of exporting. The training will be delivered through a combination of: Virtual and blended webinars. Practical sessions. Capacity-building activities. The programme identifies Modules 1–14 as part of this foundational stage. For SMEs that are still developing their understanding of international trade, this first tier provides an opportunity to strengthen the foundational knowledge required to operate across borders. Tier 2: Digital and Sector Skills Period: April – June 2027 The second tier moves beyond basic trade foundations and focuses on more advanced capabilities. The programme expects 200 SMEs to participate at this stage. Businesses selected for Tier 2 will receive support in areas including: E-commerce. Sustainability-related trade. Trade finance. Market adaptation. Regional and trade-corridor bootcamps. Targeted technical support. Mentorship. Buyer connections. Digital trade readiness. Trade finance readiness workshops. Modules 16–19 are identified for this stage, alongside additional technical and business support activities. This stage is particularly relevant to SMEs that have progressed beyond basic export knowledge and are looking to develop more specialised capabilities for entering or expanding within regional markets. Tier 3: Export Acceleration Period: July–August 2027 The third tier focuses on turning export readiness into practical commercial opportunities. The programme expects 50 SMEs to participate at this stage. Businesses reaching Tier 3 will receive support related to: Developing export plans. Accessing new markets. Securing trade finance. Transaction support. Buyer engagement. Trade finance facilitation. One-to-one sessions. Continued business development. The ICC specifically identifies Module 18 on transaction support as part of this stage. Important Progression Requirement An important point for prospective applicants is that the three tiers are not presented as separate, independent opportunities. The ICC states that only SMEs that participate in Tier 1 are eligible for Tier 2 and Tier 3 . This means that SMEs interested in progressing to the more advanced digital, sector-specific and export acceleration support should understand that participation begins with the foundational stage. Who Is TradeRoots Africa For? TradeRoots Africa is designed for African small and medium-sized enterprises that have potential to scale across African markets. The programme specifically seeks a balanced cohort comprising: Emerging SMEs Growth-stage businesses Established SMEs The common factor is the potential for these businesses to expand and scale across African markets. This means the opportunity is not limited exclusively to newly established businesses. More established SMEs can also be considered where they demonstrate the potential to expand across African markets. TradeRoots Africa and the African Continental Free Trade Area A significant component of the programme is its connection to the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) . AfCFTA is referenced by the ICC as one of the key frameworks within which TradeRoots Africa will help SMEs become export-ready. The programme also considers the role of Regional Economic Communities (RECs) , recognising that African businesses can operate within both continental and regional trade frameworks. For SMEs, understanding these frameworks can be important when considering expansion into markets beyond their home country. TradeRoots Africa therefore seeks to make trade policy more practical for businesses by connecting knowledge of continental and regional trade arrangements with practical capabilities such as export compliance, documentation, market access, logistics, digital trade and finance. What Businesses Can Gain From TradeRoots Africa The programme provides several potential areas of development for participating SMEs. Export Readiness One of the central objectives is to help businesses become better prepared for exporting. This includes understanding export compliance and documentation, as well as gaining knowledge of regional trade requirements. Market Access Businesses can develop greater awareness of opportunities to access regional and international markets. Later programme activities also include buyer connections and market adaptation support. Trade Finance Readiness TradeRoots Africa incorporates trade finance into its support framework, including dedicated trade finance readiness workshops and facilitation during the export acceleration stage. Digital Business Capabilities Businesses participating in later stages can develop capabilities relating to digital trade and e-commerce. These skills can be particularly relevant to SMEs seeking to reach customers and commercial partners beyond their traditional geographic markets. Mentorship and Technical Support Participants can benefit from mentorship and targeted technical support as they develop their trade capabilities. Buyer Connections The programme s advanced stages include buyer connections and buyer engagement, creating opportunities for participating businesses to move beyond training towards practical commercial relationships. Export Planning At the export acceleration stage, selected SMEs will work on export plans and receive support related to entering new markets. These components demonstrate that TradeRoots Africa is structured around progression from learning and capacity building towards practical export activity. Programme Stage Period Expected Participation Applications Open until 15 October 2026 — Programme launch November 2026 — Tier 1: Trade Foundations November 2026 – March 2027 1,000 SMEs Tier 2: Digital and Sector Skills April – June 2027 200 SMEs Tier 3: Export Acceleration July – August 2027 50 SMEs The programme is scheduled to run from November 2026 through August 2027 . TradeRoots Africa Application Deadline The application deadline is 15 October 2026 The ICC states that applications are currently open until 15 October and that the programme will officially launch in November 2026. Prospective applicants should therefore prepare their applications before the stated deadline rather than waiting until the final day. How to Apply for TradeRoots Africa Interested businesses can apply through the official TradeRoots Africa application channel provided by the International Chamber of Commerce. Application deadline: 15 October 2026 Applicants should review the official programme information and entry criteria carefully before submitting their application. APPLY HERE Who Qualifies for TradeRoots Africa? Based on the information provided by the ICC, the opportunity is intended for: African SMEs. Emerging SMEs. Growth-stage businesses. Established SMEs. Businesses with strong potential to scale across African markets. Businesses interested in becoming export-ready and accessing regional or international markets. African Countries and Continent Eligibility TradeRoots Africa is presented as a programme for SMEs across Africa , with the stated objective of helping African businesses compete regionally and globally. The ICC s programme information references participation through its network of national committees and African chambers. The listed partners include organisations connected with countries including Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, Morocco and South Africa , among others. Therefore, applicants from African countries should check the official application requirements to determine whether their particular business meets the programme s entry criteria. Want to understand AfCFTA opportunities. Need stronger knowledge of export compliance. Want to improve their trade documentation capabilities. Are exploring e-commerce and digital trade. Need greater awareness of trade finance. Want to identify new buyers or markets. Are developing an export strategy. Have products or services with potential for regional expansion. Want mentorship and technical support related to international trade. Are seeking to build stronger business development capabilities. The programme s three-tier structure means businesses at different stages of development can potentially engage with the programme, while the later tiers are reserved for SMEs that have participated in Tier 1. For that reason, prospective applicants should not assume additional exclusion criteria that are not stated in the available source. Businesses should review the complete official entry criteria before applying. TradeRoots Africa Partners The programme is supported through a broader network involving the ICC s global network, ICC national committees and African chambers. Kenya National Chamber of Commerce and Industry (KNCCI). Lagos Chamber of Commerce and Industry (LCCI). Japan Chamber of Commerce and Industry (JCCI). South Africa s Department of Trade, Industry and Competition (the dtic). ICC Morocco. These partnerships form part of the ecosystem supporting TradeRoots Africa. Why Export Readiness Matters for African SMEs For a business seeking to expand internationally, export readiness involves more than having a product that can be sold in another country. A business may also need to understand: Applicable trade rules. Export documentation. Customs procedures. Logistics. Market requirements. Digital tools. Financing options. Potential buyers. Regional trade arrangements. Business adaptation requirements. TradeRoots Africa brings many of these areas together within one programme. Its approach is therefore designed to help SMEs move through a progression: first developing foundational knowledge, then building more specialised capabilities, and finally working towards practical export opportunities. title: Royal Holloway University of London Announces 10 Funded PhD Studentships for 2027 Through the Social Purpose Centre for Doctoral Training
summary: Royal Holloway, University of London is inviting applications for 10 funded PhD studentships through its Social Purpose Centre for Doctoral Training (CDT) , offering doctoral researchers the opportunity to undertake research designed not only to generate new knowledge but also to deliver tangible benefits for society, communities, organisations or the environment. The 2026–27 competition supports doctoral research across an unusually broad range of disciplines, including artificial intelligence, computer science, engineering, economics, business, law, psychology, health, sociology, geography, politics, literature, culture, environmental science and biological sciences. Successful applicants will receive funding for 3.5 years full-time equivalent , covering UK-rate MPhil/PhD tuition fees together with a UKRI-rate stipend of £23,805 for the 2026/27 academic year, including London Allowance . The studentships can support full-time or part-time study, subject to the funding terms. Applicants must be eligible for UK Home fee status , and the University explicitly states that applicants assessed as overseas students are not eligible for this particular funding competition. The application deadline is 20 October 2026 , with successful candidates expected to begin their doctoral studies on 11 January 2027 . About Royal Holloway, University of London Royal Holloway, University of London is a research-intensive UK university with a substantial postgraduate research community and involvement in multiple Doctoral Training Partnerships, Doctoral Landscape Awards and Centres for Doctoral Training. The University participates in doctoral training structures including programmes associated with the Arts and Humanities Research Council, Economic and Social Research Council, Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council, Natural Environment Research Council and other UK research-funding initiatives. Beyond discipline-specific doctoral training, Royal Holloway operates researcher-development programmes intended to help postgraduate researchers build transferable professional capabilities alongside their academic expertise. The Social Purpose CDT forms part of this wider institutional approach to postgraduate research but has a distinctive requirement: doctoral research must clearly demonstrate why the research matters outside academia and how it can contribute to positive social, economic, environmental or public outcomes. What Is the Royal Holloway Social Purpose Centre for Doctoral Training? The Social Purpose Centre for Doctoral Training is designed around the principle that research should have a clearly articulated purpose beyond academic knowledge production alone. In this competition, Royal Holloway defines social-purpose research as work directed toward addressing a real-world challenge, injustice, unmet need or opportunity and capable of producing a tangible public benefit. This does not mean every project must immediately result in legislation, a new product or a direct policy intervention. Social impact can be immediate or longer-term. For example, a doctoral project might contribute to: Improving health and wellbeing Reducing economic, social or digital inequalities Addressing climate change or biodiversity loss Improving the responsible use of artificial intelligence Supporting vulnerable or marginalised communities Developing more equitable business practices Improving public policy Strengthening environmental sustainability Addressing gender inequality Developing safer digital technologies Improving access to healthcare Supporting responsible innovation Advancing cultural inclusion and community cohesion Developing technologies that can subsequently support industry, public services or society Applicants therefore need to explain not only what they want to research , but also why the research should be undertaken and who could ultimately benefit from it . 10 Funded PhD Studentships Available Royal Holloway is recruiting 10 doctoral researchers for the latest cohort of its Social Purpose CDT. These are not limited to one academic department or narrow field. Applicants can pursue research across the University s arts and humanities, social sciences, business and law, and science disciplines, provided an appropriate Royal Holloway supervisory team can support the project and the proposal demonstrates a credible social-purpose dimension. Candidates can take one of two broad approaches. They may develop their own doctoral research proposal and identify suitable Royal Holloway academics to supervise it. Alternatively, candidates can explore one of the project ideas already proposed by Royal Holloway academics and work with the relevant potential supervisor to develop that proposal into a doctoral research project. In either case, applicants cannot simply submit an application without making supervisory arrangements first. Funding Package The Social Purpose CDT studentship provides funding for 3.5 years on a full-time-equivalent basis . The award covers UK-rate MPhil/PhD tuition fees and provides a stipend set at the applicable UKRI rate. For the 2026/27 academic year , Royal Holloway states that the stipend is: £23,805 per year FTE, including London Allowance. Funding also incorporates time for a career-enhancing research placement or challenge-led activity of up to three months. Applicants should note that this award is specifically tied to UK Home tuition-fee eligibility. Royal Holloway s current applicant guidance states that it is unable to accept overseas students for this funding scheme . This restriction relates to fee status rather than race or ethnicity. Full-Time and Part-Time Study The official studentship information states that the award can fund full-time or part-time UK-rate tuition fees , with the funding period calculated on a full-time-equivalent basis. Applicants considering part-time registration should discuss the structure and feasibility of their proposed programme with the relevant department and supervisory team before applying. Mandatory Three-Month Placement or Challenge-Led Research A major feature of the Social Purpose CDT is its emphasis on applying research outside conventional academic settings. Successful postgraduate researchers are expected to undertake either a placement or a piece of challenge-led work lasting up to three months . This activity may involve a: Business organisation, public-sector institution, charity, community organisation, third-sector organisation or another relevant external partner. The objective is to allow researchers to experience how research evidence can be translated into practice while developing transferable capabilities such as leadership, stakeholder engagement and policy communication. The placement must be incorporated into the doctoral timetable so that the PhD can still be completed within the funded 3.5-year period. Training and Professional Development The Social Purpose CDT is not structured solely around the completion of a thesis. Award holders are expected to participate in the wider postgraduate researcher community and undertake additional professional and researcher-development activities. Each funded postgraduate researcher is expected to complete at least 10 days of development and training activities every year , including Social Purpose CDT cohort training. Researchers will also be expected to participate in relevant on-campus activities, cohort-development opportunities and broader programmes covering areas such as researcher development, knowledge exchange, teaching preparation and wellbeing. Royal Holloway s applicant guidance also indicates that researchers will be expected to demonstrate their learning and skills development through the University s permitted alternative thesis format. Research Supervision Requirements Every proposed project must have a supervision team consisting of at least two Royal Holloway supervisors . Applicants must therefore identify an appropriate primary supervisor and communicate with potential supervisors before submitting the formal application . The proposed supervisory team must agree that it is willing to support the application. Royal Holloway specifically instructs candidates to contact prospective supervisors directly before preparing the final submission. Applicants should not treat this as an optional networking step. Securing supervisory support is an integral component of the application process. Proposed Research Areas The current call demonstrates how broad the concept of social-purpose research can be. Royal Holloway academics are inviting applications across subjects ranging from public health and inequality to AI, economics, sustainability, digital rights and cultural studies. Examples currently highlighted by the University include research into children s education and mental health , using large administrative datasets to investigate whether educational attainment can influence later mental-health outcomes; migration, humanitarianism, reparation and cultural practice ; relationships between opera, politics and society ; care politics and the human right to care ; violence, gender inequality and social policy; and the use of intergenerational and intercultural creative practices to strengthen community cohesion . Business and management possibilities include AI adoption among SMEs, political economy, migrant and refugee entrepreneurship, precarious employment, fintech, mergers and acquisitions, banking regulation, behavioural finance, the macroeconomics of AI and geopolitics, global production networks, international migration, digital consumer behaviour, entrepreneurial learning, gig work, algorithmic management, fraud, organisational accountability, sustainability accounting, platform economies and digital technologies affecting marginalised workers . Law-focused proposals can investigate subjects including medical-device regulation, digital healthcare, telemedicine and predictive AI , including questions concerning regulation, clinical practice, patient autonomy and rights. Science and engineering opportunities include projects addressing sea-ice reflectivity and climate change , climate-resilient renewable-energy microgrids for AI data centres, eyewitness identification and face recognition, inequality in access to depression treatment, artificial intelligence for early detection of mental and metabolic disorders, lower-cost and lower-energy deep learning, secure and privacy-preserving digital communication, and vitamin-A biofortification of food crops. These topics are illustrative rather than meaning that every applicant must select one exactly as published. Royal Holloway explicitly permits applicants to develop their own proposals where an appropriate supervision team can be identified. Social Purpose Must Be Clearly Demonstrated Applicants should not treat the phrase social purpose as a generic statement about research being beneficial. Royal Holloway s guidance specifically requires proposals to demonstrate a clear connection between: The proposed research → a significant social challenge → identifiable potential beneficiaries. Applicants are expected to explain why the work matters. Examples given by Royal Holloway include research that could support sustainability, reduce inequality, respond to mental-health challenges, promote innovation or contribute to improved public or organisational outcomes. A technically strong project that fails to articulate this social-purpose relationship risks performing poorly against the competition s assessment criteria. Who Can Apply? Candidates must be capable of meeting the admission requirements of the relevant Royal Holloway MPhil/PhD programme and must be eligible for UK Home tuition-fee status. There is no single degree-subject requirement applying to all 10 studentships because proposals are being accepted from many departments. Qualifications therefore depend heavily on the chosen discipline and project. For example, the sea-ice project welcomes applicants from fields including physics, engineering, chemistry and Earth sciences, while a proposed AI-based health-detection project specifies a strong Computer Science or Engineering background with machine-learning and deep-learning expertise. Candidates should consequently check the normal PhD entry requirements of the department to which they intend to apply and discuss their academic fit with the proposed supervisor. Current Royal Holloway PhD Students Can Also Apply The competition is not restricted to completely new applicants. Royal Holloway states that currently registered, unfunded first-year PhD students may also apply. The current call gives students who began around September or October 2026 as an example of those who may qualify. Existing eligible students use a separate application route specified by the University. Application Documents Required Applicants need to prepare a substantial doctoral application. Royal Holloway s current guidance requires: Personal Statement — maximum 500 words. It should explain the candidate s motivation for doctoral study, interest in the specific project, relevant previous experience, preparedness for a PhD and what the applicant hopes to gain from doctoral training. Research Proposal — maximum four pages plus one page of references. The proposal should state that the applicant is applying for an RH PhD Social Purpose Studentship, provide a project title, include a social-purpose statement of no more than 250 words, establish the background and research gap, explain the research aim and design, provide a 3.5-year timeline including the placement, identify the supervisory team, explain required research or training resources, discuss relevant external partners where applicable and include ethical considerations of no more than 250 words. Supervisor Letter — maximum one page. The primary supervisor must assess the applicant s readiness for doctoral research, explain how the supervision team will support the researcher, address project feasibility and explain how the research connects with Royal Holloway s social-purpose objectives. Curriculum Vitae. The CV can include academic qualifications, paid and unpaid experience, publications, conference presentations, awards, recognition, training and relevant technical or professional skills. Qualification Transcripts. Applicants must provide the academic records required by the University. Applicants are also asked to complete a separate Getting to know our applicants form. Royal Holloway states that information collected through this form is intended to support monitoring of diversity and equality initiatives and does not form part of the assessed application . How to Prepare the Research Proposal The research proposal is particularly important because it carries a substantial proportion of the assessment. Applicants should clearly demonstrate that their project is intellectually credible, methodologically realistic and achievable within the funding period. The proposal needs to account for the three-month placement or challenge-led activity rather than constructing a 3.5-year research plan and attempting to add the placement afterward. Applicants should also discuss expected training, laboratory work, fieldwork, research visits or data requirements where relevant. Where external resources will be necessary, the proposal should explain where the required support is expected to come from. How Applications Will Be Assessed Royal Holloway has published a transparent weighting system for the competition. Applicant preparedness accounts for 40% of the assessment. Evaluators will consider previous academic achievements, the CV, personal statement, relevant academic, professional and life experience, and the supervisor s supporting statement. Quality and feasibility of the PhD proposal accounts for another 40%. Reviewers consider the strength and novelty of the research ideas, methodology and design, feasibility within the funded period, inclusion of the placement, potential impact, proposed supervisory expertise and practical feasibility of required research activities. Fit with Social Purpose accounts for the remaining 20%. The panel evaluates how convincingly the proposal aligns with Royal Holloway s commitment to research with meaningful societal value. This means that applicants should not concentrate solely on academic grades. A competitive submission needs to combine candidate preparedness, a credible research design and a convincing explanation of social impact. How to Apply New applicants must submit their PhD application through the Royal Holloway Applicant Portal . Before doing so, candidates should: Identify the appropriate Royal Holloway PhD programme, research potential supervisors, contact the proposed supervisor directly, develop the research proposal with an appropriate supervision team, obtain agreement from that team to support the application, prepare the required documents and complete the University s diversity-monitoring form. Applicants may submit either an independently developed proposal or one developed from a project idea advertised by an interested supervisor. Important Dates The principal dates published on Royal Holloway s current Social Purpose CDT webpage are: Application deadline: 20 October 2026 Applicants notified of outcome: 1 December 2026 Required start date: 11 January 2027 There is, however, a discrepancy worth noting. The current applicant-guidance PDF lists shortlisted interviews between 20 October and 3 November 2026 and refers to decision letters being issued on 6 November 2026 , whereas the main Royal Holloway funding page lists 1 December 2026 as the outcome-notification date. The application deadline and start date are consistent across both sources. Candidates should therefore treat 20 October 2026 as the firm application deadline and follow subsequent timing communicated directly by Royal Holloway. Applicant Information Events Royal Holloway has also scheduled online information sessions for applicants who want to better understand doctoral study or the application process. The current funding page lists sessions on: 24 September 2026, 1:30 PM–3:00 PM , and 30 September 2026, 12:30 PM–2:00 PM . The sessions cover the studentship and doctoral application process and are particularly useful for candidates preparing an application before the October deadline. Why the Placement Component Matters One of the strongest features of this competition is the deliberate link between doctoral research and organisations outside academia. A PhD candidate studying digital inequality, for example, may have an opportunity to work with a public institution or community organisation affected by technological change. A candidate researching environmental sustainability could work alongside an environmental organisation or industry partner. A researcher examining public policy, health or social inequality could engage with a government, charity or policy-oriented organisation. The purpose is not simply work experience. The placement is intended to help doctoral researchers understand how evidence is interpreted, implemented and communicated within real-world institutional settings. This practical dimension is integral to Royal Holloway s concept of a Social Purpose PhD. What Makes a Strong Application? A strong application should establish a convincing relationship between the applicant, the proposed research question, the supervisory team and the societal value of the project. The candidate should be able to explain why the research problem matters, what gap in existing knowledge will be addressed, how the research will answer the proposed question, why Royal Holloway is an appropriate environment for the project and how the findings could ultimately benefit identifiable stakeholders. Candidates should also ensure their research plan is realistic within 3.5 years. Highly ambitious projects that require inaccessible datasets, excessive fieldwork or resources without credible funding arrangements may struggle against the competition s feasibility criteria. Similarly, simply describing a project as socially important without identifying likely beneficiaries or routes to impact may not adequately address the programme s Social Purpose requirement. Deadline Applications for the 10 Royal Holloway Social Purpose CDT PhD Studentships must be submitted by 20 October 2026 . Applicants must also be able to begin the PhD on 11 January 2027 . Because applicants need supervisory agreement before applying, prospective candidates should contact potential supervisors well ahead of the deadline instead of waiting until the final days of the competition. Conclusion The Royal Holloway Social Purpose Centre for Doctoral Training 2027 PhD Studentships provide a significant funded doctoral opportunity for researchers interested in combining rigorous academic research with demonstrable public or societal impact. Ten studentships are available across a wide range of disciplines, extending from artificial intelligence, computer science, engineering and environmental science to business, economics, law, psychology, sociology, politics, culture and the humanities. Each award provides 3.5 years of funding on a full-time-equivalent basis , covers UK-rate MPhil/PhD tuition fees , and offers a 2026/27 UKRI-rate stipend of £23,805 FTE including London Allowance . Successful candidates will also undertake a placement or challenge-led project lasting up to three months and participate in structured researcher-development activities. Prospective applicants should first identify a suitable Royal Holloway supervisor and secure support from a supervision team. They must then prepare a detailed research proposal, personal statement, CV, academic transcripts and supervisor supporting letter before completing the online application. The deadline is 20 October 2026 , with funded candidates required to start on 11 January 2027 . For more global opportunities, click HERE . title: University of Cambridge MPhil in Conservation Leadership 2027: Applications Open with Full and Partial Scholarship Support
summary: Applications are now open for the University of Cambridge MPhil in Conservation Leadership for October 2027 entry , an intensive postgraduate programme designed for professionals who want to strengthen their ability to lead meaningful change in biodiversity conservation, environmental policy, conservation organisations, government, business, and the wider sustainability sector. Delivered by the University of Cambridge Department of Geography in collaboration with the Cambridge Conservation Initiative (CCI) , the programme combines academic study with leadership development, management training, consultancy work, professional mentoring, and a substantial professional placement. Applications for the 2027 intake opened on 9 September 2026 and will close on 8 December 2026 . The programme begins on 1 October 2027 . Importantly, a limited number of full and partial scholarships are available. Full scholarship support can cover university fees as well as provide a stipend toward living expenses, although funding is competitive and is not automatically awarded to every successful applicant. About the University of Cambridge MPhil in Conservation Leadership The Cambridge Masters in Conservation Leadership is an 11-month, full-time Master of Philosophy degree based within the University s Department of Geography. The programme was created to address a major challenge in global conservation: conservation professionals often need not only strong scientific or technical knowledge, but also the ability to manage organisations, influence policy, lead teams, communicate strategically, raise resources, build partnerships, manage change and operate across complex political, social and economic systems. The programme therefore places leadership and management alongside conservation knowledge. The University describes the course as intended for applicants who have at least three years of relevant professional experience and clear leadership potential . The programme normally admits approximately 20 students each year , creating a relatively small and internationally diverse cohort. Applications for the 2027 Intake Are Now Open Candidates seeking to join the programme in the 2027–2028 academic year should pay close attention to the following dates: Applications opened: 9 September 2026 Application deadline: 8 December 2026 Course funding deadline: 8 December 2026 Gates Cambridge deadline for the U.S. funding round: 14 October 2026 Course start date: 1 October 2027 Study duration: 11 months Study mode: Full-time Qualification: Master of Philosophy (MPhil) The University s course directory notes that courses can sometimes close early, so applicants should avoid leaving preparation until the final days before the deadline. What Makes the Cambridge Conservation Leadership Programme Different? A distinctive feature of the MPhil is the collaboration between the University of Cambridge and leading conservation organisations that form part of the Cambridge Conservation Initiative . Rather than limiting learning to lectures and academic assignments, the programme integrates practical conservation leadership experience into the curriculum. Students engage in: Classroom-based interdisciplinary learning Leadership and management development Group consultancy work Real-world conservation problem solving An individual professional placement Interaction with conservation practitioners and researchers Professional networking Leadership mentoring Every student also receives one-to-one mentoring from a senior leader , providing an additional professional-development component alongside the academic curriculum. Study at the David Attenborough Building The programme is based in the David Attenborough Building in Cambridge , a major centre for conservation organisations, researchers and practitioners. The MPhil has dedicated teaching space within the building, giving students regular opportunities to interact with individuals working across international conservation organisations and University research groups. This environment is particularly significant because students are not studying conservation leadership separately from conservation practice. Instead, they operate within an institutional environment where academics, NGOs, international organisations and conservation professionals are working on active biodiversity and sustainability challenges. Cambridge Conservation Initiative Partners The conservation organisations involved in the Cambridge Conservation Initiative and the broader delivery environment of the programme include organisations such as: BirdLife International British Trust for Ornithology Cambridge Conservation Forum Fauna Flora International Union for Conservation of Nature Royal Society for the Protection of Birds TRAFFIC Tropical Biology Association UN Environment Programme World Conservation Monitoring Centre Wildlife Conservation Society The programme also draws upon expertise from academic departments across the University of Cambridge. This cross-organisational structure gives students access to perspectives extending beyond traditional academic conservation science into policy, international development, NGOs, management, governance and conservation practice. Cambridge MPhil in Conservation Leadership Curriculum The programme is structured to take participants through different levels of leadership development. Students begin by examining conservation leadership itself and their own role as leaders before progressing toward leading people and organisations and ultimately influencing wider systems. The current taught curriculum contains five main modules. CL101: Conservation Leadership Problems and Practice This module establishes a common foundation in conservation leadership theory and practice. Students explore major contemporary drivers of biodiversity loss and develop an understanding of the complex ecological, political, economic and social conditions influencing conservation. The module is important because effective conservation leadership requires more than knowledge of species and ecosystems. Conservation leaders must understand the institutional and societal forces that create or intensify environmental problems. CL102: Leading Self Effective leadership begins with understanding one s own behaviour, values, strengths, weaknesses and professional objectives. The Leading Self module develops areas including: Personal resilience Reflexive practice Cultural awareness Leadership development Career planning Students are encouraged to examine how their own leadership style affects their ability to work with individuals, organisations and communities. CL103: Leading People and Organisations This module moves from individual leadership toward organisational management. Students develop knowledge and practical capabilities relating to: Strategic planning Human-resource management Fundraising Project management Organisational leadership These skills are particularly relevant for individuals who intend to lead NGOs, conservation programmes, government teams, sustainability initiatives, international projects or environmental organisations. CL104: Innovation for Conservation Leadership Conservation challenges increasingly require new approaches rather than simply repeating existing models. This module focuses on developing the ability to: Innovate Manage change Think entrepreneurially Develop practical solutions Work collaboratively on conservation challenges An important part of the module is an intensive group consultancy project conducted with a Cambridge Conservation Initiative partner organisation . This enables students to apply leadership and management concepts to an actual organisational challenge. CL105: Leading Systems Many environmental problems cannot be solved by one individual or organisation. Climate change, biodiversity loss, wildlife trade, conservation finance, governance failures and unsustainable economic activity are systemic issues involving governments, businesses, communities, civil society and international institutions. The Leading Systems module therefore examines how conservation leaders can bring about broader societal change through mechanisms including: Governance Communication Incentives Institutional influence Policy interventions Systems-level leadership The objective is to prepare participants to understand not merely how to manage a conservation organisation but how to influence the systems within which conservation organisations operate. Professional Placement: Putting Conservation Leadership into Practice One of the central components of the Cambridge MPhil in Conservation Leadership is the individual professional placement . Students work with an organisation involved in conservation practice or research and undertake a defined project dealing with a conservation leadership challenge. Professional placements are developed during the earlier stages of the course before students move more intensively into the placement period. Previous placement themes have included areas such as: Improving collaboration between conservation organisations and Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities Nature-based tourism and community resilience Illegal wildlife trade Blue-carbon finance Youth leadership in environmental organisations Ecotourism Biodiversity policy Community-led conservation Nature-positive business strategies Organisational development Previous placement hosts have included organisations such as Fauna Flora, UNEP-WCMC, Blue Ventures, BirdLife International and the British Trust for Ornithology . The placement is therefore intended to bridge the gap between leadership theory and professional conservation practice. How Students Are Assessed Formal taught coursework is concentrated primarily during the Michaelmas and Lent terms, from October to March . Students complete the same core modules, supporting peer learning within the cohort. Assessment can involve several formats, including: Coursework Written assessments Oral assessments Presentations Posters Projects Placement-related work For the professional placement component, students complete a report of no more than 4,000 words , accompanied by an oral presentation, as well as an additional piece of placement coursework of no more than 6,000 words . Students receive written feedback on submitted work and progress reporting during the programme. Who Can Apply for the MPhil in Conservation Leadership? The programme is intended primarily for professionals who already have meaningful work experience and who can demonstrate leadership potential. Applicants are expected to have at least three years of relevant postgraduate professional experience . Importantly, that experience does not necessarily have to be entirely within the conservation sector . Relevant professional backgrounds can include: Biodiversity conservation Environmental management Government Public policy Business Sustainability International development NGOs and civil society Voluntary-sector organisations Conservation research Natural-resource management Environmental governance The University specifically states that the course is designed for graduates with relevant experience in conservation, public policy, business or the voluntary sector and that professional experience does not necessarily have to come directly from conservation employment. This makes the programme potentially relevant to candidates attempting to apply leadership, governance, organisational, policy or management experience to environmental challenges. Academic Qualification Requirements Applicants are normally expected to hold at least the equivalent of a UK Good II.i Honours Degree , commonly referred to as a good upper-second-class degree or equivalent international qualification. Candidates who studied outside the United Kingdom should review the University s country-specific international qualification guidance to determine whether their academic qualifications meet the required standard. The programme combines academic selection with assessment of professional experience and leadership potential. Consequently, applicants should be prepared to demonstrate both: Sufficient academic ability to succeed in an intensive Cambridge postgraduate programme. Evidence that their previous professional experience demonstrates meaningful leadership potential. English Language Requirements Applicants who are required to demonstrate English-language competence must meet the University s course-specific standards. For the MPhil in Conservation Leadership, the published requirements include: IELTS Academic Overall score: 7.0 Listening: 7.0 Reading: 7.0 Writing: 7.0 Speaking: 7.0 TOEFL Internet-Based Test Overall score: 100 Listening: 25 Reading: 25 Writing: 25 Speaking: 25 The University also accepts specified results from C1 Advanced and C2 Proficiency , subject to its published score requirements. Candidates seeking course-specific scholarship support should note that scholarship funding can only ultimately be awarded where the candidate can demonstrate that the University s English-language requirements have been met. Full and Partial Scholarships for the Cambridge Conservation Leadership MPhil The programme has a particularly important funding component for international applicants. A limited number of scholarships are available specifically to support students admitted to the Master s. Funding can be either partial or full . According to the programme s scholarship information: Partial scholarships may cover particular components of a student s financial requirements. Full scholarships include university fees. Full scholarships also include a stipend to help cover living costs. Scholarships are competitive. Selection takes account of: Academic quality Professional experience Conservation leadership potential Priority is given particularly to candidates from countries that are rich in biodiversity but limited in financial resources , especially applicants who would otherwise be unable to finance their studies. Applicants should therefore avoid interpreting the availability of scholarships as a guarantee of funding. Admission and scholarship selection are competitive processes. How to Request Conservation Leadership Scholarship Support Candidates must first make a formal application to the MPhil through the University s postgraduate admissions system. Applicants interested in programme-specific scholarship support are then instructed to submit a financial case of no more than 200 words to the programme. The financial case should explain: Funding already available to the applicant Any funding gap Additional resources required for the applicant to accept a place Scholarship decisions are generally made between February and May for the cohort starting the following October. GEF Fonseca Leadership Fellowship: Full Funding for Eligible Candidates The Cambridge Master s in Conservation Leadership also participates in the Global Environment Facility s Fonseca Leadership Program . Under the arrangement announced by Cambridge, the Master s is scheduled to award two Fonseca Fellowships each year across three academic years: 2025–26, 2026–27 and 2027–28 . These fellowships provide full funding for Master s studies . They additionally support a three-month leadership internship following completion of the Master s degree . Candidates are selected from programme offer-holders who: Are resident in eligible GEF recipient countries Demonstrate strong emerging conservation leadership potential Would otherwise be unable to afford the programme The Fonseca Fellowship therefore represents an especially significant funding route for eligible conservation professionals from many countries in the Global South. Other Funding Opportunities Applicants are encouraged to explore multiple funding sources rather than depending exclusively on one scholarship. Potential sources identified by the programme include: Cambridge Trust scholarships Gates Cambridge Scholarships Chevening Scholarships Commonwealth Scholarships Wildlife Conservation Network Scholarship Program Russell E. Train Fellowship opportunities Other external funding schemes for which individual candidates may qualify Eligibility, deadlines and funding conditions vary considerably among these programmes, so applicants should review each scholarship separately. The official Cambridge course page gives 8 December 2026 as the course funding deadline for Michaelmas 2027 entry, while the Gates Cambridge U.S. round has an earlier deadline of 14 October 2026 . Documents Required for the Application Applications are submitted through the University of Cambridge Applicant Portal . For the MPhil in Conservation Leadership, candidates should prepare the following principal requirements: Two references Applicants must provide two referees. Depending on individual circumstances, these may be academic or professional referees. References must reach Cambridge by the course deadline. Academic transcript Applicants must provide evidence of their previous academic record. CV or résumé The CV should present the applicant s academic background, professional employment, leadership responsibilities and relevant conservation or sector experience. English-language evidence Where required, applicants must demonstrate competence in English in accordance with the University s requirements. 500-word Statement of Interest Applicants must prepare a statement entitled: Why I would like to enrol on the MPhil in Conservation Leadership and how my background provides the relevant leadership experience for this course. 500-word Sample Essay Candidates are also required to submit an academic essay analysing the major conservation leadership challenges facing a conservation organisation with which they are familiar. Widening Participation Questionnaire Applicants to the programme are currently asked to complete additional contextual information relating to previous study. Applicants seeking a Gates Cambridge Scholarship have additional Gates-specific requirements. What Makes an Application Complete? Submitting the online form alone does not necessarily complete the process. The University states that an application is complete when: The application and required supporting documents have been submitted through the Applicant Portal. The application fee has been paid where applicable. The required referees have submitted their references. Applicants should therefore contact prospective referees early rather than waiting until immediately before the deadline. Selection and Interview Process Applications for the Conservation Leadership MPhil are assessed together after the application deadline. The current selection timetable indicates that: Interviews are expected to take place in January . Conditional-offer decisions are generally made around late February . Because only around 20 students are typically admitted each year, candidates should make their application documents highly specific to conservation leadership rather than submitting a generic postgraduate personal statement. What Should Applicants Emphasise in Their Statement of Interest? The required 500-word statement provides applicants with an opportunity to connect their professional record directly with the objectives of the programme. A strong statement should clearly address: Why the applicant wants to study Conservation Leadership at Cambridge The applicant s relevant professional experience Specific examples of leadership Environmental or conservation challenges the applicant has encountered Organisational or policy responsibilities held Evidence of managing people, projects, partnerships or change The applicant s future conservation goals How Cambridge training would strengthen their ability to create impact Applicants should avoid simply repeating their CV. Instead, the statement should establish a coherent connection between previous experience, leadership potential, future ambitions and the specific training offered by the Cambridge MPhil. Preparing the 500-Word Conservation Leadership Essay The second substantial written component requires applicants to analyse the major conservation leadership challenges facing an organisation with which they are familiar. Candidates should approach this as an analytical exercise rather than merely providing a description of the organisation. Issues that could potentially be examined include: Governance Organisational strategy Community engagement Financial sustainability Human resources Institutional capacity Policy influence Stakeholder conflict Conservation effectiveness Leadership succession Organisational culture Political constraints Climate and biodiversity pressures Collaboration and partnerships Communication Fundraising The best approach will depend on the organisation selected and the applicant s familiarity with its work. What Students Are Expected to Learn By completion of the 11-month programme, students are expected to be able to evaluate different conservation tools and approaches, interpret conflicting evidence, develop practical responses to conservation problems, work across disciplinary boundaries, communicate complex information to diverse audiences and manage projects both individually and collaboratively. The programme particularly seeks to develop the ability to turn academic and theoretical understanding into practical conservation leadership. Students therefore graduate not simply with additional environmental knowledge but with training in how to organise, manage, communicate and lead interventions intended to achieve conservation outcomes. International and Diverse Cohort The Masters is explicitly international. Cambridge states that participants come from diverse backgrounds and from countries around the world. Cohorts are intentionally small, with approximately 20 students normally joining each year. Graduates join the University of Cambridge Conservation Leadership Alumni Network , which includes alumni working internationally across conservation, government, civil society, research and other sectors. The University s current postgraduate course information states that the alumni network includes graduates from 92 countries . This international peer network is a significant element of a programme intended to address environmental challenges that often cross national, institutional and disciplinary boundaries. International Student Visa Considerations International students admitted to the programme will need to ensure that they satisfy the relevant United Kingdom immigration and student-visa requirements. The programme specifically advises international candidates to review both University visa guidance and UK Government Student Visa requirements before applying. The course itself does not require ATAS clearance , according to Cambridge s current postgraduate entry information. Can Graduates Continue to a PhD? The MPhil in Conservation Leadership is primarily a professional taught Master s degree , rather than a programme specifically designed as preparation for doctoral research. Students who later wish to pursue a PhD in Geography or another relevant subject must submit a separate application through the normal University admissions process. Applicants whose principal objective is immediate doctoral research should therefore understand the professional and applied focus of the Conservation Leadership MPhil before applying. Why Professionals May Consider the Cambridge MPhil in Conservation Leadership The programme is particularly suited to people who have progressed beyond the earliest stage of their careers and are beginning to encounter more complex leadership responsibilities. Someone may possess strong technical conservation expertise but still need additional capability in: Managing teams Organisational strategy Fundraising Governance Negotiation Communication Policy influence Entrepreneurship Project leadership Stakeholder management Systems change The Cambridge programme is structured explicitly around these types of challenges. For professionals working at the intersection of biodiversity, environmental governance, policy, international development and organisational leadership, the combination of academic study, mentoring, consultancy and professional placement can provide a broader leadership-development experience than a conventional conservation-science degree. Application Deadline The application deadline for the University of Cambridge MPhil in Conservation Leadership beginning in October 2027 is 8 December 2026 . The same date is currently listed as the programme s general course funding deadline. Candidates should begin preparing well before the deadline because the application requires: References Academic records A professional CV A 500-word statement of interest A separate 500-word analytical essay Any required English-language evidence Additional scholarship documentation where applicable Applicants seeking external scholarships may also face earlier deadlines. Conclusion The University of Cambridge MPhil in Conservation Leadership 2027 offers experienced and emerging conservation leaders an opportunity to combine postgraduate academic study with applied leadership training at one of the world s leading universities. The 11-month programme differs from a conventional environmental Master s because it places substantial emphasis on leadership, organisational management, real-world conservation challenges and professional development. Students undertake interdisciplinary taught modules, an organisational consultancy project, an individual professional placement and one-to-one mentoring while studying within the David Attenborough Building and the wider Cambridge Conservation Initiative environment. A limited number of full and partial scholarships are available, with full awards covering fees and providing support toward living expenses. Priority for programme-specific scholarship support is particularly directed toward strong candidates from biodiversity-rich countries with limited financial resources. The programme also participates in the GEF Fonseca Leadership Program, which provides full funding opportunities to eligible offer-holders from GEF recipient countries. Applications for October 2027 entry are open now and close on 8 December 2026 . Candidates with a strong academic background, at least three years of relevant professional experience and demonstrated leadership potential should prepare their applications carefully and ensure that both their admission and funding requirements are completed before the applicable deadlines. title: The Africa Institute Senior and Postdoctoral Fellowships 2027 in UAE: Applications Now Open for Researchers in African and African Diaspora Studies
summary: Applications are now open for the 2027 Research Fellowships Program at The Africa Institute, Global Studies University , offering senior and postdoctoral scholars an opportunity to undertake full-time research residencies in Sharjah, United Arab Emirates . The fellowship program is designed for scholars whose research engages substantially with Africa and the African diaspora , particularly across the humanities and social sciences. The 2027 call includes four named fellowships covering African diaspora literature, global African studies, visual and performance studies, critical humanities, gender, feminism, social sciences, and cultural studies. The program brings researchers into The Africa Institute’s scholarly community, where they can advance major research projects while participating in an interdisciplinary academic environment focused on Africa and its global diasporas. The Institute is part of Global Studies University and describes itself as an international center dedicated to research, documentation, study, and teaching relating to Africa and its diaspora. The application deadline is September 30, 2026, at 11:59 PM Gulf Standard Time (GST) . About The Africa Institute The Africa Institute is based in Sharjah, United Arab Emirates, and operates within Global Studies University . Its academic work focuses on expanding research, teaching, documentation, and intellectual exchange concerning Africa and African diaspora communities. Its broader academic environment includes postgraduate education as well as research activity in the humanities and social sciences. The university currently offers graduate-level study connected to Global African Studies and Global Studies, while the Institute hosts senior and postdoctoral researchers working across diverse interdisciplinary areas. The Research Fellowships Program therefore goes beyond simply providing researchers with time to work independently. Fellows become part of an established scholarly environment in which research on Africa and its diaspora is examined through historical, cultural, literary, artistic, political, social, and interdisciplinary perspectives. The Four Research Fellowships Available for 2027 The 2027 Research Fellowships Program consists of two Senior Fellowships and two Postdoctoral Fellowships . 1. Toni Morrison Senior Fellowship in African Diaspora Literature and Cultural Studies Named in honor of the celebrated author and Nobel Prize laureate Toni Morrison , this fellowship focuses particularly on areas connected with African diaspora literature, culture, cultural studies, and related intellectual fields. The opportunity is intended for established scholars, including academics at the associate professor or full professor level and comparable scholars working outside conventional university positions. Independent authors and public intellectuals whose work has received significant recognition in relevant fields may also fall within the intended applicant profile.
